title: The as-if rule and compile-time optimization
recap: The as-if rule permits a compiler to transform a program in any way that does not change its observable behavior. Constant folding, constant propagation, and dead-code elimination are common optimization techniques.

Optimization lets programmers favor readable, maintainable expressions. Whether a particular expression is optimized is compiler- and build-dependent, so correctness tests should verify observable behavior rather than optimizer internals.
objectives: Express a fixed total as a readable calculation from named constants.
Build a second calculation from previously named results.
Treat exact program output as the observable behavior that must be preserved.
Avoid build-mode branches or attempts to detect a specific optimization.
warnings: The as-if rule does not guarantee that a particular optimization will occur.
Timing, assembly inspection, and optimizer-specific macros are not portable correctness tests.
Debug and release builds must not intentionally produce different observable output.
challenge: Repair the bakery calculations using named const int values. Compute bakedMuffins as trays * rowsPerTray * muffinsPerRow, compute reservedMuffins as 2 * muffinsPerRow, and subtract that named amount to obtain packedMuffins. Keep the same observable output in every build mode; test the values, not whether the compiler folds them.
hints: A tray has rows and each row has muffins, so the baked total combines all three named dimensions with multiplication.
Give the two reserved rows their own value by multiplying 2 by muffinsPerRow.
Initialize packedMuffins by subtracting reservedMuffins from bakedMuffins; no build-mode condition or optimizer probe is needed.

contains: const int bakedMuffins{ trays * rowsPerTray * muffinsPerRow };
